los.text: Recognise the structure and describe movements of the hip joint (including the bones fused to create the acetabulum)
los.html:
TypeSynovial ball and socket; the femoral head sits deep in the acetabulum.
AcetabulumFormed by the ilium, ischium and pubis, which meet at the Y-shaped triradiate cartilage (fuses around 15–17 years).
Deepened byThe fibrocartilage labrum and the transverse acetabular ligament.
Ligament of the head (ligamentum teres)Carries a small artery, important in children, minor in adults.
MovementRange
Flexion~120° (knee bent)
Extension~20°
Abduction / adduction~45° / ~30°
Medial / lateral rotation~35° / ~45°

los.text: Identify and explain the actions of the muscles on the hip joint, including flexors, extensors, abductors, medial rotators, adductors and lateral rotators
los.html:
MovementMusclesNerve
FlexionIliopsoas (strongest), rectus femoris, sartorius, pectineusFemoral; psoas from L1–3 directly
ExtensionGluteus maximus (climbing, rising from sitting), hamstringsInferior gluteal (L5–S2); sciatic
AbductionGluteus medius and minimus, tensor fasciae lataeSuperior gluteal (L4–S1)
AdductionAdductor longus, brevis and magnus, gracilis, pectineusObturator (hamstring part of magnus: tibial)
Medial rotationAnterior fibres of gluteus medius and minimus, TFLSuperior gluteal
Lateral rotationPiriformis, obturator internus, gemelli, quadratus femoris, obturator externus, gluteus maximusNerves from the sacral plexus

los.text: Describe the structures responsible for the stability of the hip joint and their relative contribution to maintaining the lower limb in different positions
los.html:
• Bony fit: the deep acetabulum and labrum hold more than half the head; the most stable joint in the body.
LigamentAttachesLimits
Iliofemoral (Y ligament of Bigelow)AIIS → intertrochanteric lineHyperextension; strongest ligament in the body
PubofemoralPubis → neckAbduction
IschiofemoralIschium → neckMedial rotation
StandingThe line of gravity falls behind the hip, so body weight pushes the hip into extension and the iliofemoral ligament takes the load with little muscle work.
Close-packed (most stable)Extension, medial rotation, abduction. Least stable: flexed and adducted (dashboard injury → posterior dislocation, sciatic nerve at risk).
Single-leg stanceGluteus medius and minimus of the standing leg hold the pelvis level (Trendelenburg).
Femoral head blood supplyMainly the medial circumflex femoral artery (retinacular branches along the neck) → displaced intracapsular neck fractures cause avascular necrosis (hence hemiarthroplasty).

los.text: Describe the sites of venous access that can be used for 'cut-down' procedures in emergencies
los.html:
SiteLandmarkNote
Great saphenous vein at the ankle~1 cm in front of and above the medial malleolusMost reliable site; saphenous nerve lies with it
Great saphenous at the groin~3–4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle (saphenous opening)Large vein, high flow
Femoral veinMedial to the femoral artery pulse just below the inguinal ligamentNAVY lateral → medial: nerve, artery, vein, Y-fronts
Basilic / cephalic / median cubital veinsAntecubital fossaUpper limb alternatives
  • Femoral artery pulse: at the midinguinal point (halfway between ASIS and pubic symphysis).

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the gluteal (buttock) region and the course of the sciatic nerve within it, explaining how to avoid it when giving intramuscular injections
los.html:
• Muscles: gluteus maximus (superficial), medius, minimus; piriformis is the landmark of the region.
Above piriformis (greater sciatic foramen)Below piriformis
Superior gluteal nerve and vessels
  • Inferior gluteal nerve and vessels
  • Sciatic nerve
  • Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
  • Pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels
  • Nerves to obturator internus and quadratus femoris
Sciatic nerve course
  • Leaves below piriformis
  • → runs down midway between the greater trochanter and ischial tuberosity, deep to gluteus maximus
  • → back of the thigh on adductor magnus
  • → splits above the popliteal fossa.
IM injections
  • Use the upper outer quadrant of the buttock (or the ventrogluteal site in gluteus medius, between ASIS, iliac tubercle and greater trochanter).
  • The sciatic nerve lies below a line from the PSIS to the greater trochanter, in the lower medial area.

los.text: Outline the origin of the lumbosacral plexus, the formation of its major branches and the structures they supply
los.html:
PlexusRootsBranches
Lumbar (forms in psoas)T12–L4 anterior ramiIliohypogastric (L1), ilioinguinal (L1), genitofemoral (L1–2), lateral femoral cutaneous (L2–3), femoral (L2–4, posterior divisions), obturator (L2–4, anterior divisions)
Sacral (on piriformis)L4–S4 (lumbosacral trunk L4–5 joins)Sciatic (L4–S3), superior gluteal (L4–S1), inferior gluteal (L5–S2), posterior femoral cutaneous (S1–3), pudendal (S2–4)
  • Femoral nerve emerges lateral to psoas; obturator medial; the lumbosacral trunk crosses the pelvic brim to the sacral plexus.

los.text: Recognise the origin, course and function of the sciatic, femoral, obturator, common peroneal (fibular) and tibial nerves, sural and saphenous nerves and summarise the muscles and muscle groups that each supplies as well as their sensory distribution
los.html:
NerveCourseMotorSensory
Femoral (L2–4)Lateral to psoas → under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral arteryQuadriceps, sartorius, pectineus, iliacusAnterior thigh
Saphenous (femoral)Adductor canal → with the great saphenous veinNoneMedial leg and foot
Obturator (L2–4)Medial to psoas → obturator canalAdductors, gracilis, obturator externusPatch of medial thigh
Sciatic (L4–S3)Below piriformis → back of thigh → splits at the top of the popliteal fossaHamstrings, hamstring part of adductor magnusVia its branches
Tibial (L4–S3)Popliteal fossa → deep to soleus → behind the medial malleolus (tarsal tunnel) → plantar nervesCalf (plantarflexors, toe flexors, tibialis posterior), soleSole
Common fibular (L4–S2)Along biceps → round the fibular neck → splitsSuperficial: fibularis longus and brevis (eversion); deep: tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL (dorsiflexion)Superficial: lateral leg and dorsum of foot; deep: 1st web space
SuralFrom tibial and common fibular branches → with the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolusNoneLateral foot; used for nerve grafts and biopsy

los.text: Explain the anatomical basis for the loss of function resulting from common nerve injuries in the lower limb (sciatic, superior gluteal, tibial and common peroneal (fibular) nerves)
los.html:
Nerve injuredCommon causeLossSign
SciaticPosterior hip dislocation, hip replacement, misplaced injectionKnee flexion, all movement below the kneeFoot drop; numb below the knee except the medial side (saphenous)
Superior glutealInjection, hip surgeryGluteus medius and minimusTrendelenburg sign: pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg; waddling gait
TibialPopliteal fossa injury, tarsal tunnelPlantarflexion, toe flexionCan't stand on tiptoe; numb sole
Common fibularFibular neck fracture, tight cast, crossed legsDorsiflexion and eversionFoot drop, high-stepping gait, foot inverted; numb dorsum of foot

los.text: Describe the dermatomes of the lower limb and outline the sensory nerve supply with respect to assessing spinal injuries
los.html:
DermatomeArea
L1Groin
L2Upper anterior thigh
L3Lower anterior thigh, knee
L4Medial leg, medial malleolus
L5Lateral leg, dorsum of foot, big toe
S1Lateral foot, little toe, heel
S2Back of the thigh
S3–5Perianal (saddle) area
Spinal injuryMap the lowest normal dermatome; saddle anaesthesia suggests cauda equina syndrome.
Dermatome vs nerveL5 root loss covers the big toe and dorsum; common fibular loss spares the sole and adds weak eversion.

los.text: Outline the segmental values for movements and reflexes at the hip, knee, ankle and foot
Recognise structures of the hip and lower limb on radiographs
los.html:
AP pelvisFemoral head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, acetabulum, obturator foramen, pubic rami, pubic symphysis, sacroiliac joints, sacrum.
Shenton's line
  • Smooth arc along the underside of the femoral neck and top of the obturator foramen
  • Broken in a neck of femur fracture, dislocation or developmental dysplasia.
Lesser trochanterLooks bigger when the leg is externally rotated (as in a hip fracture: shortened, externally rotated leg).
AlwaysLook at both hips, and get a lateral view; fractures can be hidden on one view.
